# Hand Poke

> 28 traditions of marking skin by hand — who is marked, who does the marking, and where on the body

130 records, bilingual English and Thai, every claim tiered and sourced. Built 2026-09-19 22:37. A companion page sits on wichaa.net.

## Findings
- **The tattoo is clothing.** 5 traditions on this site have a source that compares the finished work to a garment, in four languages across three centuries, plus a Cordilleran rule recorded in English: Burmese thigh work as "a skin-tight pair of caleçons" (1882), Lanna work as "black trousers", Visayan work as "a kind of handsome armor", and untattooed Samoan and Cordilleran men as naked, in the ordinary word. Printed with each quote at /clothing/.
- **The leg-tattoo zone crosses modern Thailand rather than stopping at its border.** Burma, the Shan States and Lanna tattooed men from the waist down; Milne's 1910 line that "the Siamese tattoo themselves very slightly, or not at all" is a statement about central Siam, not about Lanna, which was a tributary kingdom until 1899. Drawn at /legs/.
- **13 of 28 traditions have a Wikipedia article about the tattooing itself**; for the other 15 it is a section inside an article about the people. Counted in language editions at /coverage/.
- **In 4,710 transcribed pages of the wichaa.net manuscript corpus, สักขาลาย — the Lanna leg tattoo — appears on 1.** Counted at /legs/.
- **72 of the marks recorded here go on skin that clothing covers and 40 on skin it does not** — and the bans land almost entirely on the second kind. At /body/.

# Records

## Ainu anchi-piri (tradition/ainu-anchi-piri)
### what
Hokkaido and Sakhalin: a woman's mouth ringed with indigo, begun in childhood and widened until she was ready to marry.
### story
The Ainu word *anchi-piri* carries the tool inside it — obsidian, and a cut. Ink came from the indigo plant. The mark was made by women on women, on the mouth, the forearms and the backs of the hands, and it grew with its owner: a small mark at five to thirteen, widened over years, finished when she married.

The Japanese state prohibited it. What happened next is the same everywhere on this site: the practice stops, the women who have it grow old, and the only pictures left are the ones outsiders took.
Sources: s:wp-ainu-people, s:wp-irezumi

## Amazigh marks (tradition/amazigh-marks)
### what
North Africa: women's chin, forehead and hand marks, in a geometric vocabulary shared with weaving and pottery.
### story
The motifs are the same motifs that appear on textiles and on painted pottery, which is the pattern seen in the Philippines too: the tattoo is not a separate art but the same design language put on a person.

*Inference —* a great deal of what is published about the meanings of these marks is collected from outside and late. This record says what the marks look like and where they go, and holds off on what each one meant.
Sources: s:wp-berbers

## Atayal ptasan (tradition/atayal-ptasan)
### what
Taiwan: a band down the forehead, and a second mark earned — by a man for taking a head, by a woman for mastering the loom.
### story
The rule was a gate. No face marks, no marriage; no face marks, no crossing to the ancestors at death. A girl learned to weave at ten or twelve and had to master it before her cheeks were marked, which makes the tattoo a certificate of competence held on the most visible surface a person has.

Japan banned it in 1930. Christianity finished the job. The marks are now on elderly faces and on the museum wall.
Sources: s:wp-atayal-people, s:wp-taiwanese-indigenous-peoples

## Batok (tradition/batok)
### what
The Philippine traditions, tapped with a hafted thorn at ninety to a hundred and twenty strikes a minute.
### story
The Spanish called the Visayans *Pintados*, the painted ones, and recorded the tattoo as dress: a naked man "appears to be dressed in a kind of handsome armor engraved with very fine work" — worn at home with nothing but a loincloth, because the marks were the clothes.

The method is Austronesian and it is not poking. A needle — thorn, bone, horn, bamboo — is set perpendicular to a wooden handle in an L, and a second stick taps the handle. The hand that holds the tool never pushes; it positions. Ink is soot or ash in water, oil, cane juice or pig bile, and the design is laid out first in ink with a blade of grass or a length of string.

Among Cordilleran peoples tattoos were a form of clothing in the same explicit sense: to have none was to be naked. Chest work was not applied to a man until he had taken a head — which is why copying those designs today is held to be a bad idea, and why the men who fought in the 1960s and 70s were advised by elders not to take them.
### today
Whang-od is ninety-something and tattooing in Buscalan; her apprentices are women, which breaks the inheritance rule her own community ran on, and her community accepted it. Around her there is a revival with a problem inside it: which designs are open.
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-whang-od, s:wp-kalinga-province

## Chin facial tattooing (tradition/chin-ming)
### what
Women's faces, marked between fifteen and twenty, in a pattern that names the tribe: full-face, part-face, dots, lines, or both.
### story
The designs differ by group and the differences are the point. M'kaan, Daai and Yin Du women are tattooed across the whole face; N'men and Matu women on certain parts of it; the Uppriu cover the face in dots; Ngagah mix vertical lines with dots; Daai set dots among vertical and horizontal lines on forehead and cheeks. Mro women wear small marks or stars on cheek, forehead or breast and tie them to fertility.

The explanation attached to the custom in almost every outside source is abduction: that a king took a beautiful Chin woman, that she disguised herself to get home, and that families marked their daughters so that no one would carry them off. The nineteenth-century British gazetteer repeats the abduction story and then adds that the anxiety "seems hardly justified by any beauty in the women themselves."

*Inference —* that sentence is worth leaving in. It is the clearest single demonstration on this site of what the colonial record is: the only written source for a great deal of this, and written by men who held the people they were describing in contempt. Read the fact, discount the frame.
### today
Banned in the 1960s and discouraged by missionaries before that, the practice ended inside one generation. The women who carry it are elderly, and they are photographed constantly by visitors to the Chin hills. Whether that is documentation or a trade in faces is not a question this site settles.
### notes
Northern and southern Chin groups differ; this record does not flatten sixty sub-groups into one design.
Sources: s:wp-chin-people, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar, s:gazetteer-1, s:gazetteer-3

## The pilgrim's cross (tradition/coptic-pilgrim)
### what
Jerusalem and Egypt: a cross on the inside of the wrist, marking a pilgrimage — and a family that has been doing it for around seven hundred years.
### story
The Razzouk family carries the trade from Egypt to Jerusalem and still holds the carved olive-wood blocks that print the designs onto the skin before the needle follows. Coptic Christians in Egypt wear the wrist cross as an everyday identification, not only as a souvenir of a journey.

*Inference —* the wooden design blocks are the same idea as the Borneo stamp and the Burmese sample book: a hand tradition that needs a repertoire invents a way to store it outside a person's memory.
Sources: s:wp-razzouk-tattoo, s:wp-copts

## Deq (tradition/deq)
### what
Kurdistan: marks on women's faces, hands and feet, for protection, for health, and to say which tribe.
### story
The word comes from Syriac *dyoqo*, puncturing — another tradition that names the tattoo after the movement of the needle. A male tattooist is *deqqak*, a female one *deqqake*; the practice predates Christianity, Yazidism and Islam in the region, and rules attach to it, including who may not receive it.
Sources: s:wp-deq-tattoo, s:wp-kurds

## Derung face marks (tradition/derung-face)
### what
Yunnan: Derung women marked on the face at twelve or thirteen, in a tradition now carried by a handful of elders.
### story
The same abduction story attaches here as in the Chin hills — that the marks were meant to make a woman unattractive to raiders. *Inference —* the story turns up wherever a colonising or dominant neighbour is in the picture, and it is always told about the women of the smaller group. It may be true in some places. It is also the explanation most convenient to everyone except the women wearing the marks.
Sources: s:wp-derung-people

## Godna (tradition/godna)
### what
Northern and central India: women's marks, pricked by women, carried out of India to the Caribbean by indentured labour.
### story
*Godna* is the verb *to prick*, which puts it in the same family as *sak*, *kaki-*, and *deq*: the word for the tattoo is the word for what the needle does. The designs go on arms, hands, legs and face, and the practice runs through Baiga, Oraon, Birhor, Munda, Santal and many other communities, each with its own repertoire.

It travelled. The tattoo went with indentured workers to Guyana and Trinidad, which makes it one of very few traditions on this site with a diaspora that kept the marks.
Sources: s:wp-godna, s:wp-munda-people

## Hajichi (tradition/hajichi)
### what
The Ryukyu Islands: marks on the backs of women's hands, outlawed by Japan in 1899 and now being put back on.
### story
*Hajichi* went on the hands, where nothing conceals them, and it recorded a woman's passage — first marks in girlhood, more at betrothal, the set completed at marriage. Japan prohibited it in 1899 while assimilating the Ryukyu kingdom, and enforcement was real enough that the practice went underground and then out.

*Inference —* the ban's design is worth noticing. A mark on the hands cannot be covered by clothing, which makes it the easiest tattoo in the world to police and the hardest to keep quietly.
### notes
Okinawan women, in Okinawa and in the diaspora, have been taking hajichi up again; this site has no count of how many.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi, s:wp-meiji-era

## Hlai women's marks (tradition/hlai-marks)
### what
Hainan: Hlai women marked on face, throat, arms and legs in patterns that told one lineage from another.
### story
Chinese records notice tattooing among non-Han peoples as far north as the Yangzi in the first millennium, which is the same body of record that the Southeast Asian traditions on this site appear in — as somebody else's custom, seen from outside.
Sources: s:wp-hlai-people, s:wp-hainan, s:wp-yantra-tattooing

## Htoe kwin (tradition/htoe-kwin)
### what
Every up-country Burmese man wore one: a sheet of dark-blue animals from the navel to below the knee, begun in boyhood.
### story
Shway Yoe — the pen name of Sir James George Scott, who lived in Burma and wrote the fullest account of it in English — opens the chapter flatly: a Burmese youth counts his thigh tattooing as important as his entry into a monastery, and until it is done "there may be doubts as to his thorough manhood."

The finished work runs from a line level with the navel to just past the kneecap, and he reaches for a garment to describe it: not a marking of the skin so much as **"a skin-tight pair of caleçons, fitting better than the best glove ever made."** The figures are tigers, cats, monkeys, elephants, *nats* and *bilus* — each one framed in an oval of letters, each frame its own setting, the gaps filled with the same tracery.

The frame is the tell. The animals are not a scene; they are a repeating field of self-contained units, which is why the whole reads at a distance as cloth rather than as a picture.

*Attested —* a good *saya* carried a sample book of drawings so the boy could pick his patterns and their places before the opium went in. A tattoo studio's flash sheet, in Burma, in 1882.
### today
Lethwei fighters — Burmese bareknuckle boxers — carry the leg work as the sport's own mark, and the Wikipedia article on tattooing in Myanmar records fighters describing the sitting, up to 24 hours across both legs, as the thing to be endured without showing it. Outside the ring it is a thinning tradition rather than a general one.
### notes
Shway Yoe reports and then refuses a claim: that the custom began for a "shameful reason assigned by foreign writers." He does not repeat the reason and says no Burman believes it. This site does the same.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar, s:gazetteer-2, s:milne-shans

## Iban tattooing (tradition/iban-borneo)
### what
Borneo: tapped designs carved on a block and printed onto the skin, with hand marks reserved for a man who had taken a head.
### story
The Iban mark a journey. *Bungai terung*, the aubergine flower, goes on each shoulder when a young man leaves on *bejalai* — the walkabout that makes him an adult. The *entegulun*, the hand tattoo, is not a decoration: it records that the wearer took a head. Anthony Bourdain filmed one of the last men entitled to it.

The design source is the striking part. Borneo tattooists carved patterns onto wooden blocks, inked the block, printed it onto the skin, and then tapped along the printed line — a stamp, a stencil and a tool in one, and a way of keeping a repertoire that does not depend on memory.
### notes
Hose and McDougall, 1912, are the fullest colonial description and carry the usual freight; the Iban record their own designs now.
Sources: s:wp-iban-people, s:hose-borneo-2

## Irezumi (tradition/irezumi)
### what
Japan: needles bound with silk to a wooden rod, worked by hand — *tebori*, carving by hand — over years, in a design that covers the body like a garment.
### story
The word says the method: *irezumi*, inserting ink. Nara ink goes grey-blue under the skin. A full back piece is not a session but a relationship, and the shape it takes — shoulders, chest panels, a gap down the sternum — is a suit of clothes that can be closed over.

The Meiji government outlawed it while courting foreign opinion, and foreigners promptly came to Japan to be tattooed. The occupation legalised it in 1948. Japanese law then held for decades that tattooing needed a medical licence, until a 2020 decision ended that. The criminal association it acquired under the ban has outlived the ban by seventy years.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi, s:wp-horimono, s:wp-yakuza

## Kakiniit (tradition/kakiniit)
### what
Inuit tattoos: women's work on women's skin, stitched with a sooted thread drawn under the skin, or poked.
### story
The method is the rarest on this site. A needle carries a sinew thread blackened with soot and is drawn *through* the skin, leaving the pigment behind it in a line — sewing, with the line left in. The same hands did the sewing that kept people alive in a cold place.

The marks answered to Sedna, whose severed fingers became the sea animals: hand and arm tattoos refer to where her hands were cut. A woman without hand marks was refused the good afterlife; a woman without face marks went to the land of the crestfallen, where the smoke rises from her throat and her head hangs down.

Then missionaries, the schools, and a century of silence. The revival is recent, documented and deliberate: Hovak Johnston's project began putting traditional marks back on Inuit women in 2016, learning the stitch from the elders who still remembered it.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit, s:wp-inuit

## Cordilleran whatok (tradition/kalinga-cordillera)
### what
The Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, where Spanish rule never reached and the tattooing was never interrupted.
### story
Cordilleran mummies in cave and hanging-coffin burials carry tattoos going back to the thirteenth century, individualised, covering an adult woman's arms and an adult man's whole body — and the coffins carry the patterns carved on the outside.

Headhunting chest work went first, when headhunting stopped. Arm and decorative work lasted longer. Elders among the Bontoc and Kalinga still carry it; among the Kankanaey, Apayao and Ibaloi it is believed gone.
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-kalinga-people, s:wp-bontoc-people

## Kayan tattooing (tradition/kayan-borneo)
### what
Upriver Borneo, where the tattooists were women and the work went on a woman's forearms, thighs and feet across years.
### story
Hose and McDougall set down the sequence, the fees and the taboos in 1912 — which is why a practice that thinned out is describable at all, and also why the description is an outsider's. The Kayan of Borneo are not the Kayan of Myanmar; the names collide and the peoples do not.
Sources: s:wp-kayan-people-borneo, s:hose-borneo-2

## Konyak marks (tradition/konyak-naga)
### what
Nagaland and across the Myanmar border: chest and face marks a man received for taking a head.
### story
*Inference —* a tattoo that certifies an act ends when the act ends. The Konyak marks, the Cordilleran chest work and the Iban hand tattoo are three unrelated traditions with the same structural weakness, and all three stopped within decades of headhunting being suppressed. A tattoo for beauty or for protection can survive a change of government. A tattoo that is a record cannot.
Sources: s:wp-konyak-naga, s:wp-naga-people

## Patutiki (tradition/marquesan-patutiki)
### what
The Marquesas: coverage so complete that Willowdean Handy's 1922 survey had to be drawn panel by panel to record it.
### story
Handy's *Tattooing in the Marquesas* is a Bishop Museum bulletin, out of copyright, and it is a catalogue of motifs recorded when very few marked people were left. The name says the method: *patu tiki*, to strike the image.
Sources: s:handy-marquesas, s:wp-marquesas-islands

## Mentawai titi (tradition/mentawai-titi)
### what
The Mentawai islands, west of Sumatra: long lines laid along arms, chest and legs, added to at each stage of a life.
### story
*Inference —* the Mentawai case is the clearest example of a pattern this site keeps meeting: a tradition is called dying for a century and is still there, thinner, with the elders carrying it and the state having spent decades discouraging it.
Sources: s:wp-mentawai-people

## Sak kha lai (tradition/sak-kha-lai)
Thai: สักขาลาย
### what
The Lanna leg tattoo: waist to knee, sometimes to the ankle, dense enough that the murals paint it as a pair of black trousers.
### story
A Lanna volume held in the wichaa.net manuscript corpus puts it plainly: temple murals show northern Thai men tattooed *จนดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ* — "until it looked as if they wore black trousers." Elders quoted in the same passage give the extent: the legs in patterns from the waist down to the ankles, the torso front and back, the arms, even the fingers; some as far as the neck and the crown of the head.

The enforcement was talk. A man who did not tattoo his legs and torso "would be gossiped about as being like a woman — lacking the endurance to bear the needle"; if he had no marks he might as well put on a *sin*, the woman's wrapped skirt. The work went to a master in the community and the fee had a Lanna name of its own, **khan tang** (ขันตั้ง), where central Thai says *khan khru*.

*Inference —* the tradition is described here in the past tense by its own inheritors, not by an outside authority, and nothing in the passage names a law. What it names is electric light: the old night courtship ended, the reason a young man needed to be looked at ended with it, and the marks went out of use within about a generation.
### today
Sak kha lai is not what a visitor to Chiang Mai is offered. What is offered is **sak yant** — the same needle, a different job. The leg tattoo covered a man; the yant marks him with a formula.
### notes
This site treats sak kha lai and sak yant as two traditions on one hand, not one tradition with two names. That separation is the client's correction, and it is the same separation the Burmese record makes between the thigh work and the charms.
Sources: s:ms6968, s:corpus, s:thwp-ล-านนา, s:milne-shans

## Sak yant (tradition/sak-yant)
Thai: สักยันต์
### what
Letters, numbers and figures arranged into a diagram — *yant* — and pricked into skin with a long needle.
### story
*Sak* is the verb: to prick. The Khmer root *cɔkʔ* means the same, and the Khmer dictionary keeps the word native rather than borrowed from Sanskrit. *Yant* is the diagram — the same word as Sanskrit *yantra*, the same family as the yantra drawn on cloth, on brass, on paper.

The Lanna volume explains why it moved to skin at all, and the reason is logistics: a yant on paper or metal is left at home. A yant on the body is carried. Everything else — which formula, which animal, which direction the letters run — follows from that one decision.

Two corrections this site carries, both from the client and both checkable. **Most sak yant is not done at Wat Bang Phra.** That temple is what the film crews know; the ordinary route is an ajarn or a monk near where you live. And **Khom is not "what a yant is written in."** Khom script is the central Thai convention. In the north the letters are northern Thai — *tua mueang*, the Tai Tham script — or Shan, or Tai Lue.
### today
Chiang Mai has working masters, and one operation there publishes the lineage of every one of them — who taught whom, which temple, how many years in the robe and how many out. That published lineage is the closest thing this site has to a family tree for a living hand tradition.
### notes
The designs themselves are indexed on wichaa.net at /yant: 36 named designs across 63 plates, entered by what each one is for.
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing, s:ms6968, s:sycm, s:thwp-การส-กย-นต-

## Shan leg tattooing (tradition/shan-tattooing)
Thai: การสักของไทใหญ่
### what
The same leg work as the Burmese, carried further — to the ankles, up the back, and on the specialists who tattooed everybody else's charms.
### story
Leslie Milne lived among the northern Shan and published *Shans at Home* in 1910. Her sentence on status is the whole of it: **a Shan boy is a child until he is tattooed.** Plucky boys start at twelve, most wait until fourteen. The rule is both legs, waist to knee, the thighs completely covered in dark blue — and often on to the ankles. Backs come later, in blue or more often red, and without symmetry: a grid of lettered squares under one shoulder blade, small circles or beasts on the other side.

Shway Yoe, writing thirty years earlier, says the Shans tattoo more extensively than the Burmese, with rays running up from the waistline to the chest and nearly to the nape, and that the retainers of a *sawbwa* — a Shan chief — might be marked everywhere but the palms and the soles.

The second thing he says is the one that matters for the whole region: **the men who tattoo charms and cabalistic figures are mostly Shans.** They are credited with the special skill, they mutter the spells over the medicine, and they are held in some awe for it. The Lanna volume agrees from the other side of the border: this fashion was widespread among the Burmese and the Tai Yai, who tattoo yantras no less than the Lanna do.
### today
Tai Yai communities span the Myanmar–Thailand border, including Mae Hong Son. This site has no count of who is still tattooed and does not guess at one.
Sources: s:milne-shans, s:shway-yoe, s:gazetteer-2, s:ms6968

## Sicanje (tradition/sicanje)
### what
Bosnia: Catholic girls' forearms and hands marked with crosses, circles and fences, pricked with soot and honey.
### story
Two nineteenth-century observers recorded it — the archaeologist Ćiro Truhelka, who drew the designs, and a doctor, Leopold Glück, who published a paper in Vienna in 1894 titled *The Tattooing of Skin Among the Catholics of Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The custom went out after the Second World War. What survives is the design vocabulary, now being applied by machine by tattooists in Croatia and Bosnia — a revival of the pattern without the practice, which is a distinct thing and this site counts it separately.
Sources: s:wp-sicanje, s:wp-croats-of-bosnia-and-herzegovina

## Stick and poke (tradition/stick-and-poke)
### what
The one everybody has seen: a needle, ink, no machine — punk kitchens, prisons, and now studios that do nothing else.
### story
Two lineages meet here and they are not the same thing. One is improvised: a sewing needle or a safety pin, ballpoint ink, done by a friend, associated with prisons and with people too young to be tattooed legally. The other is professional hand-poke, done with medical needles in a studio, which is now a standing style with its own practitioners.

*Inference —* this site lists it as a tradition because it is one, and because the same word covers both ends of it. The difference between the two is not the method; it is whether the needle is sterile and whether the person holding it has been taught.
Sources: s:wp-stick-and-poke, s:wp-prison-tattooing, s:wp-russian-criminal-tattoos

## Tā moko (tradition/ta-moko)
### what
New Zealand: albatross-bone chisels struck with a mallet, cutting a groove that stays visible as texture, not only as colour.
### story
*Tā moko* is not a puncture. The *uhi* — a hafted chisel of albatross bone — is struck, and the skin keeps the furrow. That is why a moko reads in raking light and why a photograph flattens it.

Pigment: *awheto*, a caterpillar fungus, for the body; *ngarehu*, burnt timber, for the darker face colour; soot from burnt kauri gum mixed with fat. It was kept in carved vessels called *oko* which were buried between uses and handed down.

Steel needles arrived with Europeans and were faster and safer, and the groove went. Men's moko had largely stopped by the 1860s; women kept receiving *moko kauae* into the twentieth century, and Michael King interviewed more than seventy women in the early 1970s who had been marked before the Tohunga Suppression Act of 1907. Since 1990 the practice has come back, machine mostly, chisel too, with women among the practitioners — and a Māori foreign minister and a prime-time news anchor wearing *moko kauae* on the country's screens.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko, s:wp-m-ori-people

## Tatau (tradition/tatau)
### what
Samoa: a comb of bone and turtle shell, struck with a mallet, covering a man from the middle of the back to the knees.
### story
The English word *tattoo* comes from this word. The *tufuga tā tatau* works with two assistants, the *'au toso*, who stretch the skin and wipe; the titles are hereditary in two families, the Sa Su'a of Savai'i and the Sa Tulou'ena of Upolu, and Samoan masters tattooed Tongan and Fijian chiefly families too.

The clothing logic is explicit here as well: an untattooed Samoan man is *telefua* or *telenoa* — naked. A man who starts the *pe'a* and cannot finish carries *pe'a mutu*, an unfinished tattoo, and that is a mark of shame that the finished work is designed to prevent.

Samoa credits Fiji with the origin, in a song about twin sisters who swam across with a basket of tools, singing that only women should be tattooed — and arrived singing the opposite.
Sources: s:wp-pe-a, s:turner-samoa

## Veiqia (tradition/veiqia)
### what
Fiji: girls marked at puberty by older women called *dauveiqia*, paid in tapa cloth and whale teeth.
### story
By 1908 there was one recorded practitioner left — a woman called Rabali, tattooing until about 1910. That is as close as this site gets to a date for the end of a tradition, and it comes with a name.

The revival is as precisely dated. The Veiqia Project, a collective of Fijian women artists, took the practice up from the archives and the objects in the 2010s. Samoa's own origin story sends the tatau across from Fiji, which makes the revived practice older than the one that borrowed it.
Sources: s:wp-veiqia, s:wp-fiji

## Cut (method/cut)
Thai: กรีด
### what
The skin is cut or chiselled and pigment is rubbed into the cut, so the mark has a texture as well as a colour.
### story
Māori *tā moko* is the clearest case: the *uhi*, a hafted chisel of albatross bone, is struck with a mallet and the skin keeps a groove. A moko made this way catches light. A moko made with a needle does not, which is exactly what changed when steel arrived — and why some practitioners have taken the chisel up again.

The Ainu word *anchi-piri* names obsidian and a cut. Among the Lumad and Negrito peoples of the Philippines a hafted chisel incises the skin in short dashes, and the result is partly scarification.
### notes
Cutting shades into scarification, which is a different practice with a different point. The test used here: if pigment is put into the wound to be seen afterwards, it is on this site.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko, s:wp-batok, s:wp-scarification

## Machine (method/machine)
Thai: เครื่องสัก
### what
An electric motor drives the needle, at speeds between fifty and three thousand insertions a minute. It is here for contrast.
### story
Until 1891 there was no need for the phrase *hand-poked*. Every tattoo in every tradition on this site was made by hand, and the differences that mattered were between a comb and a point, a chisel and a needle.

*Inference —* the machine did not only speed the work up; it renamed everything else. "Traditional", "hand", "by hand" are all retroactive labels, applied after a machine existed to distinguish them from. That is worth holding on to when a tradition is described as having "resisted" the machine: most of them had no opinion about a device that did not exist when the practice was formed.
Sources: s:wp-tattoo-machine, s:wp-samuel-oreilly

## Poke (method/poke)
Thai: แทง
### what
A point held in the hand and pushed into the skin, once per mark, with the pigment carried on or into the hole.
### story
The hand does the work: it provides the force, the depth and the rhythm. A poked line is a row of punctures close enough to read as continuous — Shway Yoe's description of the Burmese method is exactly that, "a series of punctures close together, forming what afterwards fades into a rough line."

The tool can be a thorn, a fish bone, a sewing needle, a sharpened bamboo splint or a two-foot weighted brass rod. What makes it poking is that nothing strikes the tool and nothing drives it but the hand.
### how
Depth is the whole skill. Too shallow and the mark leaves with the skin; too deep and the pigment spreads under it and the line thickens with age.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-stick-and-poke

## Stitch (method/stitch)
Thai: ร้อยด้าย
### what
A needle carrying a thread blackened with soot, drawn through the skin so the line of pigment stays where the thread passed.
### story
Skin stitching is the Arctic method, and it belongs to the same set of hands and the same needle case as the sewing that made the clothing people survived in. Nothing is punctured repeatedly; the line goes in once.

It is the rarest method on this site — two traditions out of the whole map — and the one that most clearly cannot be done by machine.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit

## Tap (method/tap)
Thai: ตอก
### what
A needle or a comb of needles fixed at a right angle to a handle, and a second piece of wood striking the handle to drive it in.
### story
This is the Austronesian method, and it runs from Taiwan through the Philippines and Borneo across the whole Pacific: Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, the Marquesas, Hawaii. The rate is about 90 to 120 taps a minute, which is a drum tempo, and the sound is what a tattooing session sounds like in half the traditions on this site.

*Inference —* the hand that holds the comb does not push. It positions and holds the angle; the striking hand supplies the force. That division of labour is what lets a wide comb lay down a band of solid black at a speed no single point can match, and it is why the Pacific traditions cover so much more skin than the poking ones.
### notes
This site keeps tapping separate from poking rather than folding both into "hand-poked". They are different tools, different rates and different results, and the traditions that use them know the difference.
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-pe-a

## Au (tool/au)
### what
A set of combs — wide ones for filling, narrow ones for line — each hafted at a right angle and struck with a light mallet.
### story
The set is the point. A *tufuga* carries combs of several widths, the way a printer carries type sizes, and the *pe'a*'s solid bands come from the wide ones. The mallet is called the *sausau*. Two assistants, the *'au toso*, stretch the skin and wipe.

The tools were made of bone, turtle shell and wood; the titles that go with them are hereditary in two families.
Sources: s:wp-pe-a

## The design block (tool/design-block)
### what
Not a needle: a carved wooden block, inked and printed onto the skin, so the tattooist follows a line instead of remembering one.
### story
Three traditions on this site solved the same problem the same way and had no contact with each other. Borneo tattooists carved designs into wooden blocks, printed them onto the skin and tapped along the print. The Razzouk family in Jerusalem still holds olive-wood blocks three hundred years old and still prints pilgrims' crosses from them. And Shway Yoe reports that a good Burmese *saya* carried **a sample book of drawings** so the boy could choose his figures and their positions before the opium went in.

*Inference —* a flash sheet, a stencil and a catalogue are all the same invention, and it arrives wherever a hand tradition has more designs than one person can hold.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-razzouk-tattoo, s:wp-iban-people

## Gisi and pat-ik (tool/gisi-pat-ik)
### what
A citrus thorn — or a bundle of them — lashed at a right angle to a short stick, tapped by a second stick.
### story
The ink is soot and water, carried in a coconut shell or a bowl, and the design is drawn on first with a blade of grass dipped in it. The needles were also made of wood, horn, bone, ivory, metal and bamboo, depending on where you were.

Archaeology backs the tool up: chisel and serrated heads of probable hafted tattoo instruments were excavated at Arku Cave in Cagayan and dated before 1500 BCE — comb-type tattoo chisels, in northern Luzon, three and a half thousand years ago.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## Hnitkwasok (tool/hnitkwasok)
### what
A brass rod about two feet long, weighted at the top with a cast figure, with a split four-way point at the other end.
### story
Shway Yoe describes it part by part in 1882 and the design is a solved problem. The *yat*, the style, is solid with a round sharp point, split into four by long slits at right angles — the slits hold the pigment, so the tool carries its own ink. The style is about four inches and fits into a hollow pipe, which joins it to the weighted end. **The weight is at the top and the length is hollow**, so the tool has mass where mass helps and none where it would tire the hand.

The weight is cast as a bird, a *nat* or a *bilu*, and a good *saya*'s is carved elaborately. The tattooist catches the shaft in his right hand and rests the point in a fork made by the left forefinger and thumb, the left hand flat on the body — the hand becomes the guide rail.
### how
Ink is lampblack from burnt sesame oil, mixed with water as it is wanted. The outline goes on first with a camel-hair brush.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## Khem sak (tool/khem-sak)
Thai: เข็มสัก
### what
The sak yant needle: a long steel or brass shaft, pushed with one hand and steered with the other.
### story
The grip is the same one Shway Yoe drew in Burma and the same one a visitor photographs in Chiang Mai today — the driving hand, the guiding fork of finger and thumb, the skin pulled tight by an assistant or by the bearer's own posture. A single design takes a sitting.

The modern working needle is steel, single-use, and that is the part of the practice that has changed most in fifty years.
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing, s:sycm, s:shway-yoe

## Lek char (tool/lek-char)
Thai: เหล็กจาร
### what
The northern instrument: an iron stylus of the kind used to incise palm-leaf manuscripts, taken to skin.
### story
The word *char* (จาร) is the verb for writing on a palm leaf with a stylus — scoring the surface and rubbing soot into the score so the letters appear. The same word, the same tool family, and in the north the same people: the men who could write the letters were the men who could put them on a body.

*Inference —* that overlap explains something about the region's tattooing that a picture of a tiger does not. A Lanna yant is a written document. The tool is a pen, the surface is a person, and the fee has the same name as a teacher's fee because the transaction is a teaching one.
### notes
Ten pages of the manuscript corpus this site counted carry the word เหล็กจาร. None of them is a tattooing manual; they are about writing.
Sources: s:corpus, s:ms6968, s:thwp-อ-กษรธรรมล-านนา

## Needle and sinew (tool/needle-and-sinew)
### what
The same needle that sewed the clothing, threaded with sinew blackened in soot and drawn under the skin.
### story
Skin stitching leaves the pigment on the thread's path. It is also the reason the practice belonged to women: the needle case was theirs, the skill was theirs, and sewing was the technology the household ran on.

A poked method existed alongside it; the revival teaches both.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit

## Nomi (tool/nomi)
### what
A wooden rod with a group of needles bound to the end in silk, pushed at a shallow angle rather than straight down.
### story
*Tebori* means carving by hand. The angle is what separates it from every other poking tool on this site: the needles go in obliquely, which is how the method lays the graded blacks that Japanese work is built on.

A machine can outline faster. Practitioners who keep the rod usually keep it for the shading.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi, s:wp-horimono

## Uhi (tool/uhi)
### what
A chisel of albatross bone hafted to a handle and struck with a mallet, cutting a groove that the pigment fills.
### story
Pigment lived in carved vessels called *oko*, buried between uses and passed down the generations. A feeding funnel, the *kōrere*, was used while a face was healing.

Steel needles replaced the *uhi* in the late nineteenth century: faster, safer, and smooth. In 2007 it was reported back in use by some practitioners.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko

## Awheto and ngarehu (ink/awheto-ngarehu)
### what
Two pigments for two jobs: *awheto*, a caterpillar fungus, for the body; *ngarehu*, burnt timber, for the darker face colour.
### story
Soot from burnt kauri gum, mixed with fat, was used as well. The pigment was kept in carved *oko* vessels, buried between uses and handed on.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko

## Indigo (ink/indigo)
Thai: คราม
### what
Pigment from the indigo plant, used by the Ainu and reported for the blue lines on Chin women's faces.
### story
Ainu and Ryukyuan tattooing both use indigo rather than soot, in islands where indigo dyeing is also the textile tradition. The same plant, the same vats, a different surface.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi, s:wp-ainu-people, s:wp-indigo-dye, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## Lampblack (ink/lampblack)
Thai: เขม่าตะเกียง
### what
Soot collected from a lamp, mixed with water as it is needed. Under the skin it reads blue-black, and it does not leave.
### story
Shway Yoe names the grade: the best lampblack is the soot of burning sesame oil. The Burmese black recipe recorded on the Myanmar article is more elaborate — soot mixed with dried gallbladder of fish or cattle, powdered, boiled, simmered with bitter melon leaves and dried to a paste until wanted.

The two colours behaved differently and everyone noticed. Milne, on the Shan: tattooing in red sometimes fades, the blue appears to be indelible. Shway Yoe, on the Burmese: the blue dye from the lampblack never disappears, the vermilion gradually fades away.

*Inference —* that difference decided what each colour was used for. Identity, manhood and the leg work went in black, for life. Charms went in red, and a charm that fades is a charm that can be renewed — which is a feature, not a fault.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar, s:milne-shans, s:wp-soot

## Nara ink (ink/nara-ink)
### what
The ink used in Japanese hand tattooing, which reads blue-grey under the skin rather than flat black.
### story
It is the pigment the whole look depends on: the graded washes of a full back piece are a property of this ink worked at this angle.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi

## Pen ink (ink/pen-ink)
### what
Ballpoint ink, India ink or whatever is to hand — the modern improvised pigment.
### story
It is not made to go into skin and it is the part of improvised tattooing that professionals raise first. Professional hand-poke uses tattoo ink and single-use needles; the method is the same, the supply chain is not.
Sources: s:wp-stick-and-poke, s:wp-tattoo-ink

## Soot and honey (ink/soot-honey)
### what
Soot, honey and sometimes saliva, pricked in with a needle.
### story
Recorded in the 1890s by the two men who wrote the practice down — a doctor and an archaeologist.
Sources: s:wp-sicanje

## Soot and milk (ink/soot-milk)
### what
Soot mixed with breast milk, reported as the Kurdish preparation.
### story
*Inference —* the additive in every one of these recipes is something sticky and mildly antiseptic that the household already has: milk, honey, bile, fat, oil. The carbon does the marking; the liquid decides how it handles.
Sources: s:wp-deq-tattoo

## Soot and water (ink/soot-water)
### what
Ash or soot from a fire, ground and mixed with water, oil, plant juice or animal bile.
### story
Across the whole map the base ingredient is carbon and the variable is the liquid. The Philippines: soot or ashes with water, oil, plant extracts like sugarcane juice, or pig bile. Kurdistan: soot with breast milk, reportedly. Bosnia: soot with honey, and sometimes saliva. Ötzi's marks were made from soot or fireplace ash.

*Inference —* carbon is the pigment every human group already had. Any fire makes it, it does not fade, and the particle is large enough to stay where it is put. Nothing else available before industrial chemistry does all three.
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-tzi, s:wp-sicanje, s:wp-deq-tattoo, s:wp-carbon-black

## Vermilion (ink/vermilion)
Thai: ชาด
### what
Cinnabar red, diluted, mixed with herbs and other things, and used for charms rather than for the standing marks.
### story
Shway Yoe: all the more important charms are reserved for other parts of the body and executed in vermilion. The *a-nu se*, the drug of tenderness, is vermilion mixed with herbs and the dried skin of the *tokay* gecko; a few dots in a triangle between the eyes are enough.

It fades — everybody says so — and a fading charm gets redone.

*Attested —* the mercury in cinnabar is toxic. The sources this site quotes do not raise that, and it is not offered here as advice about anything; it is a fact about the pigment named in them.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-cinnabar, s:wp-vermilion, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## The aubergine flower (motif/bungai-terung)
### what
*Bungai terung*, worn on each shoulder when a young Iban man leaves home on his journey.
### story
A spiral at the centre stands for the tendril of a pumpkin plant; the mark is put on before the journey, not after it. A tattoo that anticipates rather than records.
Sources: s:wp-iban-people

## Cats and monkeys (motif/cat-monkey)
### what
The two commonest figures on a Burmese thigh, named in the same breath as tigers and elephants.
### story
The name of the animal is often written inside the figure as well, which Shway Yoe compares, drily, to a child labelling a drawing.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## The face grids (motif/chin-grid)
### what
Lines, dots, and combinations of both, arranged differently by each Chin group.
### story
Full face, part face, all dots, vertical lines with dots, stars on cheek and forehead. Sixty sub-groups, and the design is the group's name written where nobody can mistake it.
Sources: s:wp-chin-people

## The framed animal (motif/framed-animal)
### what
A tiger, a cat, a monkey, an elephant, a *nat* or a *bilu*, each sitting inside an oval frame of letters.
### story
Shway Yoe: each representation is surrounded by a roughly oval tracery of letters, which forms a curious and remarkably effective frame, so each animal has a setting of its own — and vacant spaces are filled the same way, the top and bottom finished with a scalloped line.

Sometimes the letters are said to carry a cabalistic meaning; ordinarily, he says, no more is claimed for them than beauty. The serious charms go elsewhere on the body, usually in vermilion.

*Inference —* the frame is what makes the leg read as cloth. A repeating field of bounded units is a textile pattern; a scene is a picture. These traditions chose the textile.
Sources: s:shway-yoe

## The centipede (motif/gayaman)
### what
The centipede, one of the standing Cordilleran figures, alongside snakes, eagles, ferns, rice grains and mountains.
### story
The motifs are the motifs of the weaving and the pottery. A tattoo tradition in the Philippines is not a separate art with its own vocabulary; it is the same vocabulary applied to a person.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## Hanuman (motif/hanuman)
### what
The monkey general of the Ramakien, and one of the standing figures of Thai yant work.
### story
A figure from the epic used as a protective device, in the same family as the Burmese *bilu* and the Shan animal syllables. The figures travel; the grammar around them does not.
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing

## Moko kauae (motif/moko-kauae)
### what
The Māori chin marking worn by women.
### story
Michael King interviewed more than seventy women in the 1970s who had received it before 1907. Since the 1990s it has been worn by a foreign minister and a prime-time news anchor, which is a change in where the mark is allowed to be seen rather than in the mark.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko

## The lettered square (motif/mystic-square)
### what
A grid of letters or numerals, read as a formula rather than as a picture.
### story
The Lanna volume notes which numerals go in: **Burmese numerals**, which the Lanna call *hora* numerals and hold to be the right ones for saiyasat rites, while the Lanna numerals — *lek nai tham* — are kept for inscribing the dhamma. Two number systems, two jobs, on one page and on one body.

*Attested —* the same book says early Lanna took these beliefs from Pagan and then developed its own forms.
Sources: s:ms6968

## The pilgrim's cross (motif/pilgrim-cross)
### what
A small cross on the inside of the wrist, printed from a carved block and then marked in.
### story
Some of the Razzouk family's blocks are three centuries old, which makes the design older than most of the tattoo machines that now apply it.
Sources: s:wp-razzouk-tattoo

## Sedna's hands (motif/sedna-hands)
### what
Hand and arm marks referring to where the sea goddess's fingers were cut off.
### story
Sedna's severed fingers became the sea animals. A woman without hand marks was refused the good afterlife; one without face marks went to the land of the crestfallen. The marks are a passport as much as an ornament.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit

## Khan tang (rite/khan-tang)
Thai: ขันตั้ง
### what
The fee, set by the master, presented in a bowl: flowers, candles, incense, cloth, coins, and whatever else that master's line asks for.
### story
The Lanna volume gives the word and the mechanism in one line: the man goes to a community master expert in yant tattooing, and there is a teacher's fee, *khan tang*, as the master sets it.

*Khan* is the pedestalled bowl. *Tang* is to set up. The same word covers the offering that opens a course of study in any Lanna craft — which is the tell: **the transaction is not a purchase, it is an enrolment.** Central Thai calls the same thing *khan khru*.

A price list is a different object and it exists too; a Chiang Mai operation publishes one. This site keeps the two apart rather than translating one into the other.
Sources: s:ms6968, s:sycm

## The rules (rite/kho-ham)
Thai: ข้อห้าม
### what
A yant works while its bearer keeps the rules that came with it — most often a list of foods not eaten and things not done.
### story
The condition is the structure. A tattoo that has to be maintained by conduct is a contract with a term, and it explains why these traditions can be strict about who receives what: the mark is the easy part and the keeping is the rest of it.

The same logic runs through the Burmese charms, which are renewed when they fade, and through the Fijian and Samoan fee, which is paid before the work rather than after.
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing

## Bearing it (rite/the-pain)
### what
In tradition after tradition the pain is not a side effect of the mark. It is the thing being demonstrated.
### story
Burma: the boy is put under opium, and some parents refuse it, and a few boys have died of the dose. Three or four figures at a sitting. The Shan: the friends sit round in a circle telling him not to scratch, that he is wriggling too much, that no girl will admire a spoiled pattern. Lethwei fighters: up to twenty-four hours across both legs, and the point is the straight face.

Samoa: a man who starts the *pe'a* and cannot finish wears *pe'a mutu*, an unfinished tattoo, and it is a mark of shame. Lanna: a man who will not bear the needle should put on a woman's skirt.

*Inference —* every tradition that uses the mark to certify endurance also needs the mark to be visible and hard to fake. That is the same reason the work is put where it cannot be hidden and takes long enough to be witnessed.
### notes
Anaesthetic, where it was used at all, was opium. No source here describes the modern options, and this site gives no advice about any of it.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:milne-shans, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar, s:wp-pe-a, s:ms6968

## When it is done (rite/the-timing)
### what
The date is rarely free. Most traditions on this site fix the work to a passage the person is making anyway.
### story
Bamar: the waist tattoo is done before or soon after temporary ordination as a monk — two rites of passage stacked on one season. Shan: twelve for the bold, fourteen for most. Chin: fifteen to twenty. Ainu: from five to thirteen, widened until marriage. Kalinga and Cordilleran: after the act that earns it. Atayal: a man's chin after he fathers a child.

*Inference —* a mark made at a moment is a dated document. It is how these traditions record a life without writing anything down.
Sources: s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar, s:milne-shans, s:wp-ainu-people, s:wp-atayal-people

## Who holds you still (rite/who-holds-you)
### what
Nobody is tattooed alone. The room is part of the method.
### story
Samoa: the *'au toso*, two assistants, stretch the skin and wipe. Fiji: one older woman applies the marks and others hold the young woman still. Burma: the tattooist's own left hand is the rest for the tool, flat against the body. Shan: the friends sit in a circle for days afterwards, because the itching is worse than the work.

*Inference —* the skin has to be tight or the point wanders, which makes at least one extra pair of hands a technical requirement rather than a social one. The witnesses come free with it.
Sources: s:wp-pe-a, s:wp-veiqia, s:shway-yoe, s:milne-shans

## Ajarn Dang and Ajarn Sak (person/ajarn-dang-sak)
Thai: อาจารย์แดง และ อาจารย์เสก
### what
Two of the Chiang Mai masters whose published profiles give a teacher, a temple, and a count of years in and out of the robe.
### story
Ajarn Dang: thirty-three years of practice, ten of them as a monk, a fifth-generation family line, trained under Sukhawaphuthargo. Ajarn Sak: eighteen years, twelve as a monk, a line through his father and grandfather, Burmese magic and the northern Tai Yai forest tradition.

That second line matters for this site's argument. A working Chiang Mai master describes his own training as Burmese and Tai Yai — which is the same border-crossing Shway Yoe described from the other side in 1882, when he wrote that the men who tattooed charms were mostly Shans.
### notes
Both tattooed this site's publisher. The pictures here that come from those sessions are used with permission and credited as such.
Sources: s:sycm, s:field-sycm

## Hovak Johnston (person/hovak-johnston)
### what
The Inuvialuk woman whose project took the kakiniit off the archive shelf and back onto skin, learning the stitch from elders.
### story
The revival has a method as well as a date: find the women who remember, learn the stitch from them, and put the marks on people who want them — starting with the women whose grandmothers had been told to stop.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit

## Leslie Milne (person/milne-shans)
### what
The ethnographer who lived among the northern Shan and published the leg-tattoo account this site leans on.
### story
Milne's book is of its period, but she stayed and she listened. The passage on tattooing carries the only direct speech this site has from inside a session: the friends sitting round the boy afterwards, telling him not to scratch, that he wriggles too much, that no girl will admire a spoiled pattern.

*Inference —* that is three sentences of what people actually said, which is more than the entire administrative record of the same decade contains.
Sources: s:milne-shans

## Rabali (person/rabali)
### what
The Fijian tattooist recorded as still working between 1908 and 1910, when she was the only one left.
### story
A tradition that ends usually ends without a date. This one has two years and a name, and that is why it sits on this site as a record rather than as a lament.
Sources: s:wp-veiqia

## Saya Chein (person/saya-chein)
### what
A Burmese tattooist named in passing in 1882 — the only working *saya* of the period this site can put a name to.
### story
Shway Yoe: "I have had fifteen figures done in little over half an hour. But then Saya Chein is a celebrated man."

That is the whole of the record. A rate, a reputation, a name, and nothing else — no dates, no village, no line of teachers. *Inference —* set that beside the Chiang Mai operation that publishes seventeen masters with their teachers, their temples and their years in the robe, and the difference is not that one tradition kept records. It is that one of them is still alive to keep them.
Sources: s:shway-yoe

## Shway Yoe (person/shway-yoe)
### what
The Scottish administrator who wrote the fullest English description of Burmese tattooing, under a Burmese pen name, in 1882.
### story
James George Scott went to Burma as a journalist, stayed as an administrator, and published *The Burman: His Life and Notions* as "Shway Yoe" — a Burmese name, on a book about Burmese life, by a man who then spent decades extending British rule over the Shan States and compiling the *Gazetteer of Upper Burma* that this site also quotes.

The chapter on tattooing is the best single source on the *htoe kwin* in English. It is also written by the administration. Both of those are true at once, and this site cites the detail while naming the hand.

*Inference —* the pen name is the thing to keep in view. A book that speaks as a Burman, written by the officer annexing the Shan States, is the whole problem of the colonial record in one byline.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:gazetteer-1

## The Sulu'ape line (person/sulu-ape)
### what
The Samoan master-tattooist titles, held in two families, and carried into the present by name.
### story
Su'a Sulu'ape Paulo II's work and life were photographed by Mark Adams; his brother Su'a Sulu'ape Petelo works at Faleasi'u on Upolu. The titles are hereditary and the *tufuga* who hold them have tattooed Tongan and Fijian chiefly families as well as Samoan ones.
Sources: s:wp-pe-a

## Truhelka and Glück (person/truhelka-gluck)
### what
The two men who recorded Bosnian sicanje in the 1890s: Ćiro Truhelka, who illustrated the designs, and Leopold Glück, who published the paper.
### story
Glück's title says exactly what it is: *Die Tätowirung der Haut bei den Katholiken Bosniens und der Herzegowina*, Vienna, 1894. A doctor and an archaeologist, writing for an Austro-Hungarian readership about the people their empire had just occupied.

*Inference —* that pairing recurs across this whole site. The professions that produced the record are medicine, administration and archaeology, which is why so much of it reads as measurement of a body rather than description of a practice.
Sources: s:wp-sicanje

## Whang-od Oggay (person/whang-od)
### what
The Kalinga *mambabatok* everyone has heard of, tapping in Buscalan since she was about fifteen.
### story
She learned from her father, and that was already an exception: only men with tattooing ancestry were supposed to learn. Her own apprentices are women, which is a second exception, and her community accepted it.

She tattooed headhunters who had earned the marks. She never married and has no children, and under the inheritance rule that would end the line — which is why the apprentices matter and why she chose them the way she did.
### notes
Buscalan now receives a stream of visitors who come to be tattooed by her. Whether that is a living tradition or a queue is argued about by people who live there, and this site does not adjudicate it.
Sources: s:wp-whang-od, s:wp-whang-od-academy

## Buscalan (place/buscalan)
### what
The village in the Kalinga highlands where batok is still tapped, and where the visitors go.
### story
Buscalan sits in Tinglayan, in mountains the Spanish never took, which is the reason there is anything left to visit.
Sources: s:wp-tinglayan, s:wp-kalinga-province

## Chiang Mai (place/chiang-mai)
Thai: เชียงใหม่
### what
The old capital of Lanna: where the leg tattoo was ordinary, where the yant is still done, and where this site is written.
### story
Two traditions and one city. The leg work is gone from it; the yant is not. The masters working here publish lineages that run back through Burmese and Tai Yai teaching, which is the border that this site's leg-tattoo map is drawn around.

The script on a northern yant is the northern script. That is the correction this site keeps repeating, because the central Thai convention gets written up as though it were the whole country's.
Sources: s:thwp-จ-งหว-ดเช-ยงใหม-, s:wp-chiang-mai, s:wp-lan-na

## Kengtung (place/kengtung)
### what
The eastern Shan town that sits in the middle of the leg-tattoo zone, and in the middle of the Tai world the zone is drawn on.
### story
Kengtung's people are Tai Khuen, whose script and manuscripts belong with Lanna's rather than with Burma's. *Inference —* the leg tattoo distribution follows this cultural geography, not the modern border: Burma, the Shan States, the Tai Khuen and Tai Lue towns, and Lanna, with central Siam outside it.
Sources: s:wp-kengtung, s:wp-khuen-people

## Mandalay (place/mandalay)
### what
Upper Burma's capital until 1885, and the centre of the country whose men were, in Shway Yoe's account, all tattooed.
### story
The contrast in his chapter is between town and country: the "puny Rangoonites" who skip the tattoo and are ashamed of it, and the *taw-tha* of the small towns and villages, not one of whom is without the dark blue tracery.

*Inference —* he is describing the beginning of the end and does not know it. Colonial rule reached the towns first, and the custom went from the towns first.
Sources: s:wp-mandalay, s:shway-yoe

## The Ukok Plateau (place/ukok)
### what
The high plateau on the Russian–Chinese–Mongolian frontier where frozen Pazyryk burials preserved tattooed skin.
### story
Water got into the burial chamber through a robber's shaft, froze, and sealed everything inside a block of ice under stone and permafrost. Clothing, wood, horses and skin came out of it.
Sources: s:wp-siberian-ice-maiden, s:wp-pazyryk-culture

## Wat Phumin (place/wat-phumin)
Thai: วัดภูมินทร์
### what
The temple in Nan whose nineteenth-century murals show northern men with their legs and torsos marked.
### story
The Lanna volume this site quotes says the evidence for the leg tattoo is in the murals of important temples, and promises examples. Wat Phumin is the best known of them: its wall paintings are the standard illustration of northern dress, northern faces and northern skin.

*Inference —* a mural is evidence that a painter expected to see marked legs, which is not quite the same as evidence of any particular man's marks. It is strong for pattern and weak for detail, and this site treats it that way.
Sources: s:thwp-ว-ดภ-ม-นทร-, s:wp-wat-phumin, s:ms6968

## anchi-piri (term/anchi-piri)
### what
Obsidian and a cut: the word carries the tool and the wound, and no word for ink.
Sources: s:wp-ainu-people

## batok (term/batok-word)
### what
From Proto-Austronesian *beCik, tattoo, with relatives *patik, mottled, and *burik, speckled — the word for a pattern, applied to skin, cloth and pot alike.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## deq (term/deq-word)
### what
From Syriac *dyoqo*, puncturing. A male tattooist is *deqqak*, a female one *deqqake*.
Sources: s:wp-deq-tattoo

## godna (term/godna-word)
### what
To prick. The noun for the tattoo and the verb for the needle are the same word.
Sources: s:wp-godna

## hajichi (term/hajichi-word)
### what
Needle-strike. Written with the characters for needle and thrust.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi

## htoe kwin (term/htoe-kwin-word)
### what
*Htoe* is to prick or pierce; *kwin* is a ring or an enclosure. The name describes the framed rings the figures sit in.
Sources: s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## irezumi (term/irezumi-word)
### what
Inserting ink. The word names the material and the direction of travel, and nothing about the hand.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi

## kakiniq (term/kakiniq)
### what
From the Proto-Inuit-Yupik root *kaki-, to pierce or prick — the same root across Iñupiaq, Inuktitut, West Greenlandic and Tunumiit.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit

## lao phung dam (term/lao-phung-dam)
Thai: ลาวพุงดำ
### what
"Black-bellied Lao" — a central Thai name for the tattooed northerner, applied from outside and carrying a view with it.
Sources: s:ms6968

## ming (term/ming)
### what
The Chin word for the facial marks. Banned by name in the 1960s.
Sources: s:wp-chin-people

## moko (term/moko)
### what
*Tā* is to strike; *moko* is the design itself. The verb in the name is the mallet, not the point.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko

## ptasan (term/ptasan)
### what
Related to the Atayal word for writing and marking — the face as a written surface.
Sources: s:wp-atayal-people

## sak kha lai (term/sak-kha-lai-word)
Thai: สักขาลาย
### what
To prick the legs in patterns — the verb, the body part and the word for pattern, in that order. No separate noun for the tattoo is needed.
Sources: s:ms6968

## sak (term/sak)
Thai: สัก
### what
To prick. The Khmer root *cɔkʔ* means the same, and the Khmer dictionary keeps it native rather than borrowed.
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing

## sicanje (term/sicanje-word)
### what
Pricking. Colloquially also *bocanje* and *bockanje*, which mean the same and sound like it.
Sources: s:wp-sicanje

## tatau (term/tatau-word)
### what
The Polynesian word English borrowed. Cook's crew wrote it down in 1769 and it displaced every English word for the practice.
Sources: s:wp-pe-a, s:wp-james-cook

## tua mueang (term/tua-mueang)
Thai: ᨲᩫ᩠ᩅᨾᩮᩬᩨᨦ
### what
The northern letters — Tai Tham script, the script of the region's manuscripts and of the yant that go on northern skin. Khom is the central convention, not the northern one.
Sources: s:thwp-อ-กษรธรรมล-านนา, s:wp-tai-tham-script

## veiqia (term/veiqia-word)
### what
The practice and the marks, in one word — and a tattooist is a *dauveiqia*, one who does veiqia.
Sources: s:wp-veiqia

## Where the marks go (story/body)
### what
Each tradition here records which zones of the body it marks. Counted together, the zones sort into two kinds.
### story
**Zones that can be covered** — thighs, back, chest, waist-to-knee — belong to traditions where the tattoo is a garment and the wearer chooses when it is seen. **Zones that cannot** — face, chin, hands, fingers — belong to traditions where the mark is an identification, and where a state that wanted the practice stopped could enforce the ban by looking at people.

*Inference —* the second group is where the bans land. Chin faces, Atayal faces, Okinawan hands, Ainu mouths, Māori chins. The leg traditions were not banned; they faded. **A mark you cannot hide is easy to police, and a mark under a longyi is not worth the trouble.**
### notes
Counted from the `placement` field on every tradition record; the chart prints how many records carried the field.
Sources: s:wp-chin-people, s:wp-atayal-people, s:wp-irezumi

## The Chin ban (story/chin-ban)
### what
Burma's socialist government banned Chin facial tattooing in the 1960s; missionaries had been discouraging it for decades already.
### story
The practice ended inside a generation. The women who carry it were tattooed as teenagers before the ban and are now in their seventies and eighties, and they are photographed constantly.

*Inference —* a ban works fastest on a mark that is made once, in youth, by a specialist. Stop the specialists for twenty years and there is nobody left who has done it.
Sources: s:wp-chin-people, s:wp-tattooing-in-myanmar

## The tattoo is clothing (story/clothing)
### what
Sources in Burmese, Northern Thai, Spanish and Samoan — and a Cordilleran rule recorded in English — reach for the same comparison: the tattoo is not on the body, it is what the body wears.
### story
Shway Yoe, Burma, 1882, on the finished *htoe kwin*: the effect is "not so much of a marking of the cuticle as of **a skin-tight pair of caleçons**, fitting better than the best glove ever made."

A Lanna volume, northern Thailand, describing the same region's work from its own side: men tattooed their bodies **จนดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ** — "until it looked as if they wore black trousers" — and a man with no marks should put on a woman's skirt instead.

A Spanish account of the Visayans: a naked tattooed man "appears to be **dressed in a kind of handsome armor** engraved with very fine work… their dress at home and in their barrio is their tattoos and a *bahag*."

The Cordillerans: having no tattoos was **equated to being naked**. The Samoans: an untattooed man is **telefua** or **telenoa** — naked, in the ordinary word, not as a figure of speech.

*Inference —* this is the one comparison that survives translation everywhere on this map, and it is doing work. A garment is the thing that makes a person presentable in public; it is put on at a particular age; its absence is shameful rather than merely unusual; and it is the first thing another person reads. Every one of those is also true of the marks. **Where a tradition covers a whole zone of the body, its own sources describe that zone as dressed.**
### notes
The count of traditions on this site whose sources use the clothing comparison is computed at build time and printed on the page rather than asserted here.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:ms6968, s:wp-batok, s:wp-pe-a

## How the word got in (story/cook-1769)
### what
English had no single word for the practice until Cook's crew brought one back from Polynesia.
### story
*Tatau* went into English as *tattoo* and swallowed everything else. Every tradition on this site is now described in English with a Samoan word, including the ones that had their own perfectly good nouns: *irezumi*, *godna*, *deq*, *kakiniq*, *sak*.

*Inference —* that is not only a linguistic accident. It is why the English-language record treats Pacific tattooing as the default case and everything else as a variation on it, and it is visible in the coverage count on this site: the traditions with the most language editions written about them are mostly the ones the eighteenth-century voyages reached first.
Sources: s:wp-james-cook, s:wp-pe-a, s:wp-joseph-banks

## Who gets written about (story/coverage)
### what
Every tradition on this site that has a Wikipedia article, ranked by how many languages wrote one.
### story
The measurement is crude and that is the point: it is a count of attention, not of importance. Each tradition here names its article, and the harvest asks the Wikimedia API how many language editions carry it.

*Inference —* the shape of the answer is predictable before you run it, which is itself the finding. The traditions with the most editions are the ones eighteenth- and nineteenth-century European voyages met first and wrote up in European languages; the ones with the fewest are inland, upland, and were written about, if at all, in an administrative report.

The Lanna leg tattoo does not appear at all. Not thinly — it has no article in any language, in a project with more than three hundred language editions, for a custom that covered the legs of every man in a kingdom.
### notes
Counted at build time. A tradition with no named article is listed as having none rather than scored as zero.
Sources: s:langlinks

## Exhibited (story/exhibited)
### what
For two and a half centuries, the main way a European saw a tattooed body was on a stage, with an entrance fee.
### story
Tattooed people from the Pacific and Southeast Asia were brought to Europe and displayed; later, European and American performers had themselves covered in order to be displayed. The human zoos and the sideshow ran on the same premise and often the same circuit.

*Inference —* a photograph of a tattooed person from this period is therefore rarely neutral evidence. It was made to be sold, the pose was chosen for the sale, and the caption was written by whoever was taking the money. This site uses those pictures where they are the only pictures, and says so beside them.
Sources: s:wp-human-zoo, s:wp-sideshow, s:wp-sailor-tattoo

## The leg-tattoo zone (story/legs)
Thai: เขตลายขา
### what
One custom, four peoples, and a boundary that runs through the middle of modern Thailand rather than along its edge.
### story
Put the sources side by side.

**Burma, 1882.** Shway Yoe: every up-country man is tattooed from the navel to below the kneecap. Not a single *taw-tha*, the sturdy man of the small towns and villages, is without it.

**The Shan States, 1910.** Milne: a Shan boy is a child until he is tattooed; the rule is both legs, waist to knee, and often on to the ankles. Shway Yoe adds that the Shans go further than the Burmese — up the back, to the nape, and among a chief's retainers, everywhere but palms and soles.

**Lanna.** The Lanna volume: men tattooed until it looked as if they wore black trousers, waist to ankle, torso, arms, fingers — and "this fashion was widespread among the Burmese and the Tai Yai, who tattoo yantras no less than the Lanna."

**Siam.** Milne, in the same paragraph where she says the Shans learned it from the Burmese: "the Siamese, who are so closely related to them, **tattoo themselves very slightly, or not at all**."

*Inference —* that last line is usually read as a fact about Thailand. It is a fact about **central** Thailand. Milne was comparing the Shan to Bangkok, and Lanna — which was a tributary kingdom, not a province, until 1899 — is on the other side of her comparison. The leg tattoo's territory is the Tai-Buddhist upland: Burma, the Shan States, the Tai Khuen and Tai Lue towns, and Lanna. **The edge of the zone runs through modern Thailand, roughly where Lanna ended, and the colonial record could not see it because it was reading the map by kingdoms.**

This is what the map on this page is drawing, and it is the one map on the site that no source draws for it.
### notes
The zone is drawn from four written sources and one manuscript. It is not a survey, nobody counted tattooed men anywhere, and the outline is this project's reading rather than anyone's measurement.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:milne-shans, s:ms6968, s:gazetteer-2, s:wp-lan-na

## Japan outlaws it (story/meiji-ban)
### what
Japan banned tattooing while presenting itself to the world, and foreigners immediately travelled there to be tattooed.
### story
The ban was about image. The practice continued underground, tattooists worked on visiting sailors and princes, and the association with criminality that the ban created outlasted the ban by three generations. Osaka's mayor was still surveying city employees about their tattoos in 2012, and the courts found against him.

The Ryukyus got their own prohibition in 1899, aimed at *hajichi* on women's hands. Taiwan's Atayal were banned from facial tattooing in 1930 by the same administration.

*Inference —* three bans, one state, sixty years, and each one targets the marks of a people being absorbed. The Meiji ban is usually told as a story about respectability. Seen with the other two, it is a story about who gets to look like themselves.
Sources: s:wp-irezumi, s:wp-meiji-era, s:wp-atayal-people

## The painted ones (story/pintados)
### what
Spain called the Visayans *Pintados*, the painted ones, described their tattoos in detail, and converted them out of the practice within two centuries.
### story
The Spanish accounts are careful and admiring. They describe the tattoo as clothing; they record that no tattooing was begun until a brave deed had been performed and that each further panel needed another; they note that men tattooed even their chins and around the eyes so that they appeared masked.

Then the same administration's church ended it. In the lowlands the tradition is gone and the description survives. In the Cordillera, where Spain never held the mountains, the practice survives and the Spanish description does not apply.

*Inference —* on this site that is the clearest natural experiment there is: one people, two zones, the same century, and the difference is entirely whether the coloniser could get there.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## Stopped, and started again (story/revival)
### what
Several traditions here stopped and came back. Where both ends are datable, this site subtracts them and prints the gap.
### story
Fiji: one tattooist left by 1908; an artists' collective takes it up again in the 2010s. Inuit: missionaries and the schools; a revitalisation project from 2016. Māori: the 1907 Act; the resurgence from 1990. Okinawa: the 1899 prohibition; hands being marked again now.

The gaps run to roughly a century each. *Inference —* what carries a practice across a hundred years is not a book. In every case on this list the bridge is a person: the elders Hovak Johnston learned the stitch from, the seventy women Michael King interviewed in the 1970s, the museum objects the Veiqia Project worked from, and the grandmothers.

A practice with no living bearer left is a different problem, and the Lanna leg tattoo is in that category.
### notes
Gaps are computed from the `break` field on each tradition and shown with both endpoints, so a reader can disagree with either.
Sources: s:wp-veiqia, s:wp-kakiniit, s:wp-t-moko

## Five thousand years (story/timeline)
### what
The dated points: bodies with marks on them, bans with statutes behind them, revivals with a year.
### story
The timeline holds three kinds of date and keeps them apart. **Bodies**: Ötzi, the Gebelein mummies, the Chinchorro man, the Ukok woman, the Cordilleran mummies, the Qilakitsoq women — each with the range its laboratory gave. **Instruments**: the Arku Cave tools. **Paper**: bans, acts, patents and the revivals.

*Inference —* the visible gap between the ancient bodies and the nineteenth-century paper is not a gap in the practice. It is a gap in what survives: skin needs ice, salt, sand or bog, and paper needs an administration. Between them, four thousand years of ordinary tattooing left neither.
Sources: s:wp-tzi, s:wp-gebelein-predynastic-mummies, s:wp-chinchorro-mummies

## The Tohunga Suppression Act (story/tohunga-act)
### what
A New Zealand statute aimed at Māori specialists, which caught tā moko along with everything else a tohunga did.
### story
Michael King interviewed more than seventy elderly women in the early 1970s who had received *moko kauae* before the Act. That interview list is the bridge: the practice was not remembered from books when it came back in the 1990s. It was remembered from faces.
Sources: s:wp-t-moko

## What the word means first (story/words)
### what
The word each tradition uses for the tattoo, and what it meant before it meant that.
### story
Four families, and they line up with the method rather than with the geography.

**Prick** — Thai and Khmer *sak*, Inuktitut *kaki-*, Hindi *godna*, Kurdish *deq*, Croatian *sicanje*, Burmese *htoe*, Okinawan *hajichi*. Every one of them is a poking tradition, and the word is the verb for what the needle does.

**Strike** — Samoan and Polynesian *tatau*, Māori *tā*, Marquesan *patu*. Every one of them is a tapping tradition, and the word is the verb for the mallet.

**Pattern** — Austronesian *batok*, *patik*, *burik*; Northern Thai *lai*. The word is the design, and it is the same word used for the pattern on a pot or a cloth.

**Write** — Atayal *ptasan*; and in Lanna, the tool for tattooing is the same *lek char* stylus used to write a palm-leaf manuscript.

*Inference —* a language names the tattoo after whichever part of it that culture finds most salient: the movement, the tool, the design, or the literacy. Four answers, and none of them is "the picture".
Sources: s:wp-yantra-tattooing, s:wp-kakiniit, s:wp-batok, s:wp-t-moko, s:wp-deq-tattoo

## The Arku Cave tools (find/arku-cave)
### what
Chisel and serrated heads of probable hafted tattooing instruments, excavated in a burial site in northern Luzon.
### story
They came up alongside adzes, spindle whorls, barkcloth beaters and lingling-o jade ornaments — the standard Austronesian kit — and they closely resemble the comb-type tattoo chisels found across Polynesia three thousand years later.

*Inference —* a tool type that travelled the whole Pacific is sitting in a cave in Luzon before 1500 BCE. The method on this site with the widest reach is also the oldest one with surviving hardware.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## Chinchorro Mo-1 T28 C22 (find/chinchorro-man)
### what
A mummified man from the Chilean coast with a dotted line tattooed above his upper lip — the oldest tattoo yet found in the Americas.
### story
The Chinchorro were mummifying their dead by about 5050 BCE, across the whole community rather than for an elite. One of the bodies carries the marks.
Sources: s:wp-chinchorro-mummies

## The Cordilleran mummies (find/cordilleran-mummies)
### what
Mummified Cordilleran people in cave and hanging-coffin burials, tattooed, with the designs also carved on the coffins.
### story
A Kankanaey mummy known as Apo Anno, 700 to 900 years old, is marked even on the soles of the feet and the fingertips. The tattoos are individualised: a woman's arms, a man's whole body.

*Inference —* when the coffin carries the same patterns as the body, the design set is doing more than decorating a person. It identifies them, to whoever opens the coffin.
Sources: s:wp-batok

## The Gebelein mummies (find/gebelein)
### what
Six naturally mummified bodies from Upper Egypt, dug out of sand graves in 1896, two of them tattooed.
### story
They were excavated by Wallis Budge for the British Museum and sat there for a century before infrared imaging showed the marks — a wild bull and a Barbary sheep on the man, S-shaped motifs on the woman.

*Inference —* that hundred-year gap is the point. The marks were on the bodies the whole time and nobody could see them, because dark pigment on darkened skin needs infrared. How much else in the world's museum drawers is tattooed and unread is not a question this site can answer.
Sources: s:wp-gebelein-predynastic-mummies, s:wp-amunet

## The Ukok woman (find/ice-maiden)
### what
