A Pazyryk woman buried on the Ukok Plateau, preserved in ice for about 2,400 years, with animal designs on her skin.
### story
An embalmed man from the same culture, at Pazyryk itself, is covered in animal motifs. The ice did the preserving, and the ice is also why the debate about where her body should now rest is a live political question rather than an academic one.

This site names the find, dates it, and leaves the reburial argument to the people whose argument it is.
Sources: s:wp-siberian-ice-maiden, s:wp-pazyryk-culture

## Ötzi (find/otzi)
### what
The Alpine body with sixty-one tattoos — nineteen groups of black lines, and the greatest concentration on the legs.
### story
The marks are 1–3 mm wide and 7–40 mm long: groups of parallel lines along the body's long axis and either side of the lumbar spine, a cross behind the right knee, another at the right ankle, parallel lines round the left wrist. Twelve of the nineteen groups are on the legs.

Microscopy on samples showed the pigment was made from fireplace soot.

*Inference —* the oldest tattooed body in Europe is a set of short lines on the legs and lower back, put there with soot. Five thousand years later, the *htoe kwin* is a leg tattoo made with lamp soot. Nothing connects them and the resemblance is not a lineage; it is what the available tools and the available pigment produce.
Sources: s:wp-tzi

## The Qilakitsoq women (find/qilakitsoq)
### what
Mummified Inuit women from north-west Greenland, five centuries old, with facial tattoos visible under infrared.
### story
They are the physical evidence behind a practice that missionaries later ended and that Inuit women have now taken up again. The revival is not reconstructing something imagined; there are faces.
Sources: s:wp-kakiniit, s:wp-mummy

## The murals (art/murals)
Thai: จิตรกรรมฝาผนัง
### what
Northern temple walls carry men with marked legs and torsos, painted by people who saw them daily.
### story
The Lanna volume rests its case on exactly this: the evidence for the custom is the murals in important temples, which show men tattooed until they look dressed.

*Inference —* a mural is good evidence for three things — that the custom existed, roughly what area of the body it covered, and that it was ordinary enough to paint without comment. It is weak evidence for the designs themselves: painters simplify, and a wall painted with a hundred figures is not a pattern book. This site reads the murals for extent and does not read them for detail.
Sources: s:ms6968, s:thwp-จ-ตรกรรมฝาผน-ง, s:wp-wat-phumin

## The sample book (art/sample-book)
### what
A book of drawings a Burmese tattooist carried, so the boy could pick his figures and their positions before the work started.
### story
Shway Yoe: "The best *sayas* carry about sample-books with them containing clever drawings, from which the aspirant may select the patterns he likes best, and mark their relative positions before he takes the opium."

That is a flash sheet, a consultation and a layout, in 1882, in a tradition usually described as though the designs came out of nowhere.
Sources: s:shway-yoe

## The stencil book (art/stencils)
Thai: แบบสักยันต์สำหรับลอกลาย
### what
A volume in the corpus this site counted is exactly what its title says: yant patterns for tattooists to trace.
### story
Its first page reads *แบบสักยันต์ · แบบยันต์ต่างๆ · สำหรับช่างสัก* — tattoo-yant patterns, various yant patterns, for tattooists. The plates are columns of Khom-script medallions under finials, birds facing each other into a heart shape, script down both sides.

*Inference —* the existence of a tracing book is the same fact as the Burmese sample book and the Bornean carved block: the repertoire is stored outside anybody's head, and it is stored in the form that transfers to skin.
Sources: s:corpus

## Sak Yant Chiang Mai (org/sak-yant-chiang-mai)
Thai: สักยันต์เชียงใหม่
### what
The Chiang Mai operation that publishes the profile of every master it works with — teacher, temple, family line, years in the robe and out.
### story
Seventeen practitioners, twelve *ajarn* and five monks; thirty teacher links; twelve named temples; family lines to the third, fourth and fifth generation.

*Inference —* that is a lineage map for a living hand tradition, published by the people in it, and there is nothing else like it on this site. Every other lineage here was reconstructed by an outsider after the fact, or lost.

It describes itself as a booking service rather than a *samnak*, a master's house, and this site repeats its own description rather than upgrading it.
Sources: s:sycm

## The Veiqia Project (org/veiqia-project)
### what
The collective of Fijian women artists who researched veiqia in collections and archives and brought the practice back.
### story
The research problem was that the practice ended around 1910 with one named practitioner. The material was in museums, in nineteenth-century accounts, and on objects. The project worked from those and from Fijian women's own reading of them.
Sources: s:wp-veiqia

## wichaa.net (org/wichaa)
Thai: วิชา
### what
The manuscript corpus and knowledge hub this site's Lanna material comes out of, and where its companion page lives.
### story
The corpus holds thousands of pages of northern Thai manuscript material, transcribed and translated, including the yant volumes indexed at /yant. The count this site publishes — how many of those transcribed pages mention the leg tattoo — was run against it.
Sources: s:corpus

## The needle now (issue/the-needle-now)
### what
Single-use needles, gloves and an autoclave are the difference between a hand tradition in 1882 and the same hand tradition today.
### story
Shway Yoe's chapter records what the old practice cost: swelling, fever, days of itching, and opium given to boys in doses that occasionally killed them. Milne's Shan boys sat in a circle being told not to scratch. None of that is nostalgia material.

The method did not have to change for that to stop; the supply did. *Inference —* this is the part of a revival that is never a reconstruction, and the practitioners doing it say so themselves.
### notes
This site carries no medical advice and no aftercare instructions, and nothing here is a recommendation about getting tattooed anywhere.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:milne-shans, s:wp-sterilization-microbiology

## The photographs (issue/the-photographs)
### what
The free pictures of tattooed bodies are mostly colonial-era photographs of people who did not choose to be photographed, or sideshow portraits made to be sold.
### story
A picture can be correctly licensed, on subject, and still be the wrong thing to put in front of a reader. This site's rules on that are simple and were set by its publisher: no blood, no wounds, nothing that turns a person into a specimen, and where a historical photograph is used, it is named for what it is.

The pictures here that show living practice were taken with permission and are credited to the people who gave it.
Sources: s:wp-human-zoo, s:commons

## What counts as hand-poked (issue/what-counts)
### what
The site is called hand poke and half the traditions on it do not poke. Here is the line it draws and why the line is arguable.
### story
A poked tattoo is driven by the hand holding the tool. A tapped one is driven by a second stick striking a hafted comb. A stitched one is sewn. A cut one is chiselled or incised and then rubbed with pigment.

All four are hand methods and none of them is a machine, which is why they are all here. But calling them all "hand-poke" flattens the thing each tradition is proudest of, so this site keeps them as four and says which is which on every record.

The hard cases are real. Māori *uhi* work was replaced by needle work in the nineteenth century and the tradition kept its name. Modern professional hand-poke uses a cartridge needle in a stabiliser pen, which is a tool with a handle and a grip and no motor. **A reader who would draw the line somewhere else is looking at the same field on the same records and can re-sort it.**
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-t-moko, s:wp-stick-and-poke

## Who wrote it down (issue/who-wrote-it-down)
### what
Most of what is known about the stopped traditions was written by the people whose arrival stopped them.
### story
Shway Yoe was Sir James George Scott, who wrote as a Burman and spent his career extending British rule over the Shan States. Leopold Glück was a doctor in occupied Bosnia. Ćiro Truhelka was an archaeologist in the same administration. Hose and McDougall were a colonial officer and a psychologist. The Gazetteer of Upper Burma is a government publication, and in the middle of a paragraph about Chin women's faces it stops to insult them.

This site uses all of it, because there is nothing else, and it names the writer every time. **The detail is usually reliable and the frame usually is not** — a measurement of a tool, a rate of work, a fee, an age, a sequence, these are the things an observer can get right. Why people did it, what they believed, what it meant: on those, the source is guessing about people it does not respect.

The Lanna volume in the corpus is the counter-case on this site, and that is why it is quoted at length: same region, same custom, written from inside it.
Sources: s:shway-yoe, s:gazetteer-3, s:wp-sicanje, s:wp-salvage-ethnography

## Whose designs (issue/whose-designs)
### what
Several traditions on this site hold that certain designs may not be worn by people who have not earned them. That rule is theirs to state and not this site's to adjudicate.
### story
Cordilleran elders hold that copying an old warrior's chest design marks a person as a killer and brings bad luck, blindness or an early death — and men who fought in the 1960s and 70s declined the marks on that advice. Kalinga inheritance rules held that tattooing could only pass down a bloodline. Sak yant carries rules the bearer keeps afterwards. *Moko kauae* is worn by Māori women.

What this site does: state the rule where a tradition states it, name who states it, and print no design as available. What this site does not do: decide who may wear what, or rank the arguments.
Sources: s:wp-batok, s:wp-whang-od, s:wp-cultural-appropriation
